label.trigger: A request gets a processing slot on the immediate path of the Throttle middleware and the wrapped handler panics, for instance a reverse proxy aborting with http.ErrAbortHandler or any handler bug caught by Recoverer mounted further out.
label.expected_impact: The slot is put back into the tokens channel by a plain statement after next.ServeHTTP, so a panic unwinds past it and the slot is gone for good. Each such panic shrinks the effective limit by one; once all slots are lost every later request waits out the backlog timeout or is rejected with 429, until the process restarts.

context_locations.note: Recoverer catches the handler panic further up the chain and answers 500, so the server keeps running with the throttle instance whose slot was never handed back.
The processing slots are created exactly once when the middleware is built; nothing ever refills the channel, so a slot that is not sent back reduces capacity permanently.

known_counterevidence.note: The path that first waits for a slot hands it back from a deferred function, so it survives a panic; a report about this branch is not the defect.
The backlog entry is released in a defer as well; only the processing slot on the immediate branch is affected.

label.fix_summary: Hand the processing slot back from a deferred function registered right after it is taken (as the waiting branch already does), so a panicking handler still returns it to the channel.

check.summary: Independent Go test: Recoverer around ThrottleBacklog(1, 0, 200ms); the first request's handler panics (500 expected), the next two requests must then get 200 instead of a 429 after the backlog wait.

verification.summary: verify --run-checks with go1.27.4: before=violation (request 2 gets 429 after the 200 ms backlog wait), after=pass. The rest of the pinned test suite still passes on the patched tree, so no existing project test notices the change; the check is an independent test copied into middleware/. The module has no dependencies; no network was used.
